Papers discussing coarse moduli spaces.

<STRUCT_0003> Keel, Mori: <EMPHOPEN_0001>Quotients in Groupoids<EMPHCLOSE_0001> <REF_0001>
<STRUCT_0004>
It had apparently long been ``folklore'' that separated Deligne-Mumford stacks
admitted coarse moduli spaces. A rigorous (although terse) proof of the
following theorem is presented here: if <MATH_0001> is an Artin stack
locally of
finite type over a Noetherian base scheme such that the inertia stack
<MATH_0002> is finite, then there exists a coarse
moduli space <MATH_0003>
with <MATH_0004> separated and <MATH_0005> an algebraic space locally of finite type over
<MATH_0006>. The hypothesis that the inertia is finite is precisely the right
condition: there exists a coarse moduli space <MATH_0007> with
<MATH_0008>
separated if and only if the inertia is finite.
<STRUCT_0005>
<STRUCT_0006> Conrad: <EMPHOPEN_0002>The Keel-Mori Theorem via Stacks<EMPHCLOSE_0002> <REF_0002>
<STRUCT_0007>
Keel and Mori's paper <REF_0003> is written in the groupoid language and
some find it challenging to grasp. Brian Conrad presents a stack-theoretic
version of the proof which is quite transparent although it uses the
sophisticated language of stacks. Conrad also removes the Noetherian
hypothesis.
<STRUCT_0008>
<STRUCT_0009> Rydh: <EMPHOPEN_0003>Existence of quotients by finite groups and coarse moduli
spaces<EMPHCLOSE_0003> <REF_0004>
<STRUCT_0010>
Rydh removes the hypothesis from <REF_0005> and <REF_0006> that
<MATH_0009>
be finitely presented over some base.

<STRUCT_0012>
Abramovich, Olsson, Vistoli: <EMPHOPEN_0004>Tame stacks in positive characteristic<EMPHCLOSE_0004>
<REF_0007>
<STRUCT_0013>
They define a <EMPHOPEN_0005>tame Artin stack<EMPHCLOSE_0005> as an Artin stack with finite inertia
such that if <MATH_0010> is the coarse moduli space,
<MATH_0011> is exact
on quasi-coherent sheaves. They prove that for an Artin stack with finite
inertia, the following are equivalent: <MATH_0012> is tame if and only
if the stabilizers of <MATH_0013> are linearly reductive
if and only if <MATH_0014> is <ACCENT_0001>tale locally on the coarse
moduli space a quotient of an affine scheme by a linearly reductive group
scheme. For a tame Artin stack, the coarse moduli space is particularly nice.
For instance, the coarse moduli space commutes with arbitrary base change while
a general coarse moduli space for an Artin stack with finite inertia will only
commute with flat base change.
<STRUCT_0014>
<STRUCT_0015> Alper: <EMPHOPEN_0006>Good moduli spaces for Artin stacks<EMPHCLOSE_0006> <REF_0008>
<STRUCT_0016>
For general Artin stacks with infinite affine stabilizer groups (which are
necessarily non-separated), coarse moduli spaces often do not exist. The
simplest example is <MATH_0015>. It is defined here that a
quasi-compact
morphism <MATH_0016> is a <EMPHOPEN_0007>good moduli space<EMPHCLOSE_0007> if
<MATH_0017> is an isomorphism and <MATH_0018> is exact on
quasi-coherent sheaves.
This notion generalizes a tame Artin stack in <REF_0009> as well as
encapsulates Mumford's geometric invariant theory: if <MATH_0019> is a reductive group
acting linearly on <MATH_0020>, then the morphism from the
quotient
stack of the semi-stable locus to the GIT quotient <MATH_0021> is a
good moduli space. The notion of a good moduli space has many nice geometric
properties: (1) <MATH_0022> is surjective, universally closed, and universally
submersive, (2) <MATH_0023> identifies points in <MATH_0024> with points in <MATH_0025> up
to
closure equivalence, (3) <MATH_0026> is universal for maps to algebraic spaces, (4)
good moduli spaces are stable under arbitrary base change, and (5) a vector
bundle on an Artin stack descends to the good moduli space if and only if the
representations are trivial at closed points.
